_readme: Hand-labelled fixtures over real BTCUSDT 4h, pivots extracted with k=3.0 ATR.
PROVENANCE WARNING: these labels were put there by the same head that wrote the algorithm,
so as an oracle they are WEAK. The user is not an Elliott analyst and cannot supply the
independent contrast, so it is replaced by three weaker oracles that at least do not share
1. `taew` (a published, independent Elliott implementation) as a differential oracle
2. the purged walk-forward over 9 years (route A of the maturity ladder)
3. the negative controls: sequences that MUST be rejected
None of them replaces a human expert. Noted here as a known limitation of the project.
A fact about the process: of 7 sequences that looked like five-wave impulses by eye, only 3
survived the hard rules. The 4 rejected ones are here as NEGATIVE cases: an engine that does
not reject is as useless as one that does not accept, and these are real market violations.

cases.notes: Bounce off the April low. It satisfies all four rules, but w3/w1=0.53 and w5/w1=0.27: wave 3 is MUCH shorter than wave 1. That is legal (R2 only forbids wave 3 from being the SHORTEST, and the shortest here is wave 5) but it is atypical of a healthy impulse. An experienced counter would probably read it as a leading diagonal or as part of a corrective of higher degree. Confidence deliberately set to medium.

The same structure carrying w5 up to the May high. REAL ambiguity, not manufactured: the same stretch admits two different endings for wave 5 and both readings are valid. It is precisely the case that forces the product to be an ORDERED set of hypotheses rather than a single answer.

Collapse from October's all-time high. w2 retraces 59.5% of w1 (a classic retracement) and w3/w1=1.48, close to 1.618. INCOMPLETE IMPULSE: exactly the case a parser without partial non-terminals would not know how to label, and where R3 and R2 are not yet evaluable.

The ALTERNATIVE reading of the same stretch, with a short w3. Wave 4 rises to 107,500, inside w1 territory (102,000-126,200). The engine has to reject it and keep the extended-w3 reading instead. That discrimination is what justifies the whole apparatus.

Recovery after the February collapse. By eye it looks like a perfect five. It breaks TWO rules: w4 enters w1 territory, and w3 is the shortest of the three. It is almost certainly a corrective of higher degree, not an impulse. It is the case that taught me most while labelling.

Second attempt at the same stretch, reading w2 as a complex corrective down to 62,510. It fixes R2 but R3 is still broken. Two different readings of the same stretch, both rejected: the stretch is NOT an impulse at this degree, and no amount of relabelling fixes that.
w4 drops to 107,245, inside w1 territory (98,200-108,790), and w3 is the shortest. The final leg of +14.9% up to 123,218 is real and large, but that does not turn what came before it into an impulse.
The March decline. w4 bounces to 87,454, inside w1 territory (81,500-95,000). Rejected.
The minimal R1 case, in a PARTIAL state. With only three vertices, R2b, R3 and R2 are not evaluable and must not invalidate anything. Checks that a partial non-terminal does not invent verdicts.
w5 (155) does not exceed w3 (160): a TRUNCATED fifth. No rule forbids it. It is flagged as exhaustion and NEVER rejected — rejecting it would throw away exactly the counts you most want near a top.
